_comment: A pre-generated card corpus. The README treats this as a first-class DX
requirement: a new developer must see a working feed without burning LLM
quota or waiting on generation. Every card here is hand-written, so the
fixture is stable, reviewable in a diff, and costs nothing to load.
Deliberately uneven: 'Distributed Systems' is thin at advanced level so the
degraded-serving path (ADR-0006) is reachable on a fresh clone rather than
being something you only meet in production.

topics.description: Container orchestration: scheduling, networking, and operations.

subtopics.title: Pods and the scheduler
subtopics.description: What a pod is, how the scheduler places it, and why placement can fail.

cards.title: A pod is the unit of scheduling
cards.summary: Kubernetes never schedules a container. It schedules a pod.
cards.body:
Kubernetes never schedules a container — it schedules a **pod**.

A pod is one or more containers that share a network namespace and storage volumes. Containers in the same pod reach each other on `localhost` and are always placed on the same node, together, or not at all.

This matters the moment you try to scale: you scale pods, not containers. If you put two things in one pod that need to scale independently, you have made a mistake that is awkward to undo later.

cards.title: The scheduler filters, then scores
cards.summary: Placement is two phases, and only the first one can fail outright.
cards.body:
Placing a pod happens in two phases.

**Filtering** removes nodes that cannot run the pod at all — insufficient CPU or memory, a taint the pod does not tolerate, an unsatisfiable node selector. If filtering removes every node, the pod stays `Pending`, and that is the failure you will actually see in practice.

**Scoring** ranks whatever survived, preferring spread across nodes and better resource fit. Scoring never fails; it only picks a winner.

So `Pending` almost always means a filter rejected everything, not that the cluster was busy.

cards.title: Requests are for the scheduler, limits are for the kernel
cards.summary: Two numbers, two completely different audiences.
cards.body:
A resource **request** is what the scheduler reserves when deciding placement. A **limit** is what the kernel enforces at runtime.

The consequences differ sharply by resource:

- Exceeding a **CPU** limit gets you throttled. Slow, but alive.
- Exceeding a **memory** limit gets you OOM-killed. Not slow. Dead.

Setting a request far below real usage is how a node ends up overcommitted and unstable — the scheduler packed it based on a number that was fiction.

cards.title: Pending is a scheduling problem, CrashLoopBackOff is yours
cards.summary: Where the pod is stuck tells you which half of the system to look at.
cards.body:
The state a stuck pod is in tells you where to look.

**Pending** — the scheduler could not place it. Nothing has run yet. Look at node capacity, taints, and node selectors. `kubectl describe pod` lists the exact filter that rejected each node.

**CrashLoopBackOff** — placement worked fine, and your container is exiting. Look at logs, the entrypoint, and config. Kubernetes is doing its job; the application is not.

Confusing these two costs more debugging time than almost anything else in Kubernetes.

cards.title: Labels are the only way things find each other
cards.summary: There are no pointers in Kubernetes. There are label selectors.
cards.body:
Nothing in Kubernetes holds a reference to a pod. A Service does not contain a list of its pods; it holds a **label selector**, and membership is recomputed continuously.

That is why a typo in a label breaks routing silently: the selector matches nothing, the Service has no endpoints, and no error is raised anywhere. Everything is behaving correctly — the set is simply empty.

`kubectl get endpoints <service>` returning nothing is the fastest way to confirm this.

subtopics.title: Services and networking
subtopics.description: How traffic reaches a pod, and what a Service actually is.

cards.title: A Service is a stable name for an unstable set
cards.summary: Pods come and go with new IPs. The Service is the fixed point.
cards.body:
Pod IPs are ephemeral. A pod restarts and gets a new one, so nothing can hold a pod IP for long and remain correct.

A **Service** provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a set of pods that is continuously re-evaluated from its label selector. Callers address the Service and never learn about individual pods.

This is why direct pod-to-pod addressing works right up until the first restart, then fails in a way that looks intermittent.

cards.title: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer are layers, not alternatives
cards.summary: Each one builds on the previous, which is why the choice is simpler than it looks.
cards.body:
The three common Service types stack:

- **ClusterIP** — reachable inside the cluster only. The default, and the base of the other two.
- **NodePort** — a ClusterIP, *plus* a port opened on every node.
- **LoadBalancer** — a NodePort, *plus* a cloud load balancer pointed at it.

So picking LoadBalancer does not replace ClusterIP; it wraps it. Knowing that makes debugging directional: if the ClusterIP does not work, the outer layers cannot.

cards.title: kube-proxy does not proxy much any more
cards.summary: The name is a historical artifact.
cards.body:
Despite the name, `kube-proxy` mostly does not sit in the data path. In its usual iptables or IPVS mode it *programs kernel rules* so traffic to a Service IP is rewritten to a pod IP, then steps aside.

The practical consequence: Service traffic is handled in the kernel, not by a userspace hop, so there is no proxy process to blame for latency. When Service routing misbehaves, the thing to inspect is the rules kube-proxy wrote, not a running proxy.

subtopics.title: Controllers and reconciliation
subtopics.description: The control loop that everything in Kubernetes is built from.

cards.title: Everything is a reconciliation loop
cards.summary: Declare the desired state; a controller works continuously to close the gap.
cards.body:
Kubernetes is not a command executor. You do not tell it to start three pods — you declare that three should exist, and a controller repeatedly compares desired state to observed state and acts to close the gap.

This explains behaviour that otherwise looks strange: delete a pod owned by a Deployment and it comes back, because nothing about your desired state changed. You deleted an *observation*, not an *intention*.

Every Kubernetes object follows this shape, which is why custom controllers feel native rather than bolted on.

cards.title: Level-triggered, not edge-triggered
cards.summary: Controllers ask 'what is true now', never 'what event fired'.
cards.body:
A controller does not act on events. It acts on **current state**.

This is level-triggered rather than edge-triggered logic, and it is why Kubernetes is robust against missed messages: if a controller misses a notification, the next resync sees the same discrepancy and fixes it anyway. Correctness does not depend on any individual event being delivered.

An edge-triggered design would need every event to arrive exactly once, which is not something a distributed system can promise.

cards.title: Deployments do not manage pods
cards.summary: There is a layer in between, and it is what makes rollbacks work.
cards.body:
A Deployment manages **ReplicaSets**; a ReplicaSet manages pods.

That middle layer is not bureaucracy. Each revision of a Deployment gets its own ReplicaSet, so a rolling update scales one up while scaling the other down, and a rollback is scaling the old one back up — the old spec still exists.

Without the intermediate object, rollback would require reconstructing the previous spec from history rather than simply pointing at a thing that is still there.

cards.title: Readiness and liveness answer different questions
cards.summary: One controls traffic, the other controls restarts. Swapping them is destructive.
cards.body:
**Readiness** asks: should this pod receive traffic right now? Failing it removes the pod from Service endpoints. Nothing is killed.

**Liveness** asks: is this process wedged beyond recovery? Failing it restarts the container.

Using a liveness probe where you meant readiness turns a slow startup or a brief dependency outage into a restart loop — and under load, into a cascading one, since every restart makes the remaining pods busier.

subtopics.title: Operating a cluster
subtopics.description: Failure modes, resource pressure, and what to check first.

cards.title: Eviction order follows QoS class
cards.summary: Under memory pressure, what dies first was decided when you wrote the manifest.
cards.body:
Under node memory pressure, the kubelet evicts by **QoS class**, which is derived from requests and limits rather than declared directly:

- **BestEffort** (no requests or limits) — evicted first.
- **Burstable** (requests < limits) — next, worst-offenders-over-request first.
- **Guaranteed** (requests == limits, for every resource and container) — last.

So the survival order of your workloads was fixed at manifest-authoring time, not at incident time. A critical service left BestEffort is first out the door.

cards.title: PodDisruptionBudgets only constrain voluntary disruption
cards.summary: A budget protects you from drains, not from crashes.
cards.body:
A PodDisruptionBudget constrains **voluntary** disruptions: node drains, cluster upgrades, anything initiated through the eviction API.

It does nothing about involuntary disruption — a node losing power, a kernel panic, an OOM kill. Those never consult it.

The common disappointment is expecting a PDB to guarantee availability. It guarantees that *you* will not take the service down during maintenance. Hardware makes its own decisions.

topics.description: Consistency, consensus, time, and failure in systems spread across machines.

subtopics.title: Failure and partial failure
subtopics.description: The defining property: some of it is broken and you cannot tell which part.

cards.title: Partial failure is the whole problem
cards.summary: A single machine is up or down. A distributed system is neither.
cards.body:
On one machine, a component is working or it is not, and your process usually finds out immediately.

Across machines, some parts work and others do not, and **you cannot reliably tell which**. A request that times out may have failed, may have succeeded with a lost reply, or may still be running.

Almost every complication in distributed systems — retries, idempotency, consensus, timeouts — exists to cope with that one ambiguity.

cards.title: A timeout is not a failure detector
cards.summary: It is a guess with a deadline attached.
cards.body:
You cannot distinguish a crashed node from a slow one. All you can do is wait a while and give up.

That makes every timeout a tradeoff rather than a setting: too short and you declare healthy nodes dead, causing spurious failovers and duplicate work; too long and real failures go unnoticed while requests pile up.

There is no correct value, only one tuned to a specific latency distribution — which is why a timeout copied from another system is usually wrong.

cards.title: At-least-once plus idempotency beats exactly-once
cards.summary: Exactly-once delivery is not available. Exactly-once *effects* are.
cards.body:
Exactly-once **delivery** across a network is not achievable: the sender cannot tell a lost message from a lost acknowledgement, so it must either risk losing the message or risk sending it twice.

What is achievable is exactly-once **effect**. Deliver at least once, and make the operation idempotent — usually by attaching a client-generated id and deduplicating on it at the receiver.

This is why so many APIs ask for an idempotency key. They are moving the problem to the layer that can actually solve it.

cards.title: Retries need backoff and jitter, not just backoff
cards.summary: Synchronised retries turn a blip into an outage.
cards.body:
When a service degrades, every client fails at once, and if they all retry on the same schedule they arrive together — repeatedly. The service is re-flattened every cycle by a thundering herd of its own making.

**Exponential backoff** spreads retries out over time. **Jitter** — randomising each delay — spreads them out relative to *each other*, which is the part that actually breaks the synchronisation.

Backoff without jitter still produces coordinated waves, just slower ones.

subtopics.title: Time and ordering
subtopics.description: Why clocks lie, and what to use instead.

cards.title: Wall clocks are not ordering
cards.summary: Two machines' clocks disagree, and one of them can run backwards.
cards.body:
Comparing timestamps from different machines to order events is unsound. Clocks drift, NTP corrections can move a clock **backwards**, and skew between machines routinely reaches milliseconds — an eternity next to a network round trip.

Use a monotonic clock for measuring elapsed time on one machine, and logical clocks for ordering across machines. Reserve wall-clock time for displaying to humans.

"Last write wins, by timestamp" is a data-loss bug wearing a conflict-resolution costume.

cards.title: Logical clocks order what actually matters
cards.summary: Causality is cheaper to track than time.
cards.body:
A **Lamport clock** is a counter incremented on each event and carried on every message; the receiver takes `max(local, received) + 1`. If A causally precedes B, A's counter is lower.

The converse does not hold: a lower counter does not prove causality, only that no causal link was recorded. **Vector clocks** recover that, at the cost of storage proportional to the number of participants.

Either way, you are tracking *happens-before* rather than *when*, which is the relation your correctness argument actually needs.

cards.title: Read-your-writes is a real guarantee with a real cost
cards.summary: Eventual consistency without session guarantees feels broken to users.
cards.body:
Under plain eventual consistency, a user can post a comment, reload, and not see it — because the read hit a replica that has not caught up. Technically correct, and it reads as a bug to everyone who is not you.

**Session guarantees** patch the worst of this: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes. They are much cheaper than full linearizability because they only constrain what one session observes.

Most "we need strong consistency" requirements are really this.

subtopics.title: Consensus
subtopics.description: Agreement despite failure — and why it is expensive.

cards.title: Quorums overlap, and that is the entire trick
cards.summary: Majority read plus majority write must share at least one node.
cards.body:
Consensus systems require a majority for writes and a majority for reads because any two majorities of the same set **must** intersect in at least one node.

That shared node is what guarantees a read sees the latest committed write. It is not a heuristic; it is set arithmetic.

It also explains why an even-sized cluster buys you nothing: six nodes tolerate the same two failures as five, while giving you one more machine that can break.

topics.description: Component-based UI: rendering, state, and the rules that keep it predictable.

subtopics.title: Rendering and state
subtopics.description: Why React re-renders when it does, and what state actually triggers.

cards.title: State updates are a request, not a promise
cards.summary: Calling a setter schedules a re-render; it does not perform one.
cards.body:
Calling a state setter does not change anything synchronously - it **schedules** a re-render. Reading the same state variable on the next line still returns the old value.

React batches these scheduled updates and re-renders once, not once per setter call inside the same event handler. This is why logging state right after setting it is a well-known trap, not a bug in your code.

cards.title: Keys tell React which item is which, not where it sits
cards.summary: An index key breaks the moment the list reorders.
cards.body:
A `key` is React's way of matching a list item across renders to the *same* underlying thing, so it can preserve state and avoid throwing DOM nodes away unnecessarily.

Using the array index as a key works only while the list never reorders or has items inserted/removed from the middle - the instant it does, React matches the wrong item to the wrong position, and component state (an open input, a checked box) jumps to the wrong row.

cards.title: Props flow down, events flow up
cards.summary: There is no other direction, and treating there as one causes most state bugs.
cards.body:
Data flows one way: a parent passes props down, a child never reaches up and changes a parent's state directly. If a child needs to affect a parent, the parent passes a callback down as a prop, and the child calls it.

Most "my state is out of sync" bugs trace back to state being duplicated in two places instead of owned in one and passed down - the fix is almost always to lift it up, not to add a sync effect.

topics.description: The database underneath: indexes, query planning, and transaction behavior.

subtopics.title: Indexes and the query planner
subtopics.description: Why an index sometimes gets ignored, and how the planner actually decides.

cards.title: An index is a bet the planner can refuse
cards.summary: Having an index does not obligate Postgres to use it.
cards.body:
The planner estimates the cost of every viable path and picks the cheapest one - an index scan is only cheaper than a sequential scan when it's expected to skip enough rows to be worth the extra I/O.

On a small table, or a query that will match most of the rows anyway, a sequential scan often wins even with a perfectly good index sitting right there. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows you the planner's actual reasoning, not a guess.

cards.title: A composite index's column order is not cosmetic
cards.summary: The index on (a, b) does not efficiently serve a query that only filters on b.
cards.body:
A B-tree composite index on `(a, b)` is sorted by `a` first, then `b` within each `a`. A query filtering only on `b` can't use it efficiently - Postgres would have to scan the whole structure.

Column order should match your most selective, most commonly-filtered-alone column first. Reordering an existing composite index to match a new query pattern is often the entire fix for a slow query, with no new index needed.

cards.title: MVCC means a delete doesn't free space immediately
cards.summary: Old row versions stick around until vacuum reclaims them.
cards.body:
Postgres's MVCC model never overwrites a row in place - an `UPDATE` writes a new row version and marks the old one dead; a `DELETE` just marks a row dead. Concurrent transactions that started before the change still need to see the old version.

`VACUUM` is what actually reclaims that dead space. Skip it (or starve autovacuum with a long-running transaction) and a table can bloat well past its live row count.

topics.description: Containers from first principles: images, layers, and what isolation actually means.

subtopics.title: Images and layers
subtopics.description: What a layer actually is, and why build order changes cache behavior.

cards.title: A layer is a diff, not a copy
cards.summary: Each Dockerfile instruction adds one, and layers below an unchanged instruction are reused.
cards.body:
Each `RUN`, `COPY`, or `ADD` instruction produces a new filesystem layer - a diff against the layer below it, not a full copy. Layers are content-addressed and cached, so if a layer's inputs haven't changed, Docker reuses it instead of rebuilding.

This is why `COPY package.json` before `COPY . .` in a Node build is the standard trick: dependency installation gets its own cached layer that survives source-code-only changes.

cards.title: A container is a process, not a lightweight VM
cards.summary: It shares the host kernel; isolation comes from namespaces and cgroups, not virtualization.
cards.body:
A container is an ordinary process on the host, isolated by Linux namespaces (its own view of processes, network, filesystem) and constrained by cgroups (CPU, memory limits). There is no hypervisor and no separate kernel.

That's why containers start in milliseconds where VMs take seconds, and also why a kernel-level exploit can escape a container in a way it never could a VM - the isolation boundary is thinner by design.

topics.description: Ownership, borrowing, and how the compiler enforces memory safety without a garbage collector.

subtopics.title: Ownership and borrowing
subtopics.description: The rule the whole language is built around, and why the compiler is so strict about it.

cards.title: Every value has exactly one owner
cards.summary: Assignment moves ownership by default; it does not copy.
cards.body:
In Rust, assigning a heap-allocated value to a new variable **moves** it - the original variable is no longer valid, and the compiler rejects any later use of it at compile time, not runtime.

This is what replaces a garbage collector: when the owner goes out of scope, Rust deterministically frees the value right there, with no separate collection pass and no doubt about when it happens.

cards.title: Borrowing lets you use a value without owning it
cards.summary: Many immutable borrows, or exactly one mutable borrow - never both at once.
cards.body:
A `&T` reference borrows a value without taking ownership. The compiler enforces one rule strictly: you can have any number of immutable borrows, **or** exactly one mutable borrow, but never both at the same time.

This single rule is what rules out data races at compile time - two threads can't both hold a mutable reference to the same data, because the borrow checker won't let the code compile in the first place.

topics.description: How packets actually move through a Linux host: sockets, netfilter, and the routing table.

subtopics.title: Sockets and the routing table
subtopics.description: What actually decides where a packet goes once it leaves a process.

cards.title: The routing table decides the exit interface before iptables sees anything
cards.summary: Routing happens first; filtering happens to whatever routing already chose.
cards.body:
A common assumption is that firewall rules decide where a packet goes. They don't - the kernel's routing table picks the outgoing interface and next hop *first*, based on the destination address, and netfilter's chains only get to accept, drop, or rewrite the packet on the path routing already chose.

This ordering is why a routing misconfiguration can look exactly like a firewall problem: the packet never reaches the interface your rules were written for.

topics.description: A query language for APIs: what problem it actually solves, and where it doesn't help.

subtopics.title: Queries and the N+1 problem
subtopics.description: Why a naive resolver setup silently turns one request into hundreds.

cards.title: GraphQL solves over-fetching, not the number of queries
cards.summary: A client asks for exactly the fields it needs - the resolver still has to fetch them from somewhere.
cards.body:
GraphQL's pitch is that a client specifies exactly the shape of data it wants, so a mobile client and a desktop client can hit the same endpoint without one of them over-fetching fields it'll throw away.

It says nothing about how many underlying database calls that costs. A naive resolver that fetches each field independently is exactly as slow as the equivalent REST N+1 problem - GraphQL just moves where in the stack that problem shows up.

cards.title: A dataloader batches what would otherwise be N separate queries
cards.summary: Per-request batching turns 'fetch this author' called 50 times into one query for 50 authors.
cards.body:
When a list of 50 posts each resolves its own `author` field independently, a naive resolver fires 50 separate 'fetch one author' queries. A **dataloader** batches all calls made within the same tick into a single `WHERE id IN (...)` query and hands each caller its slice of the result.

This is the standard fix for GraphQL's N+1 problem, and it's opt-in - nothing about the spec forces you to use one, which is why unoptimized GraphQL APIs are a very common performance complaint.
